question_text: Before he became the legendary star, X had largely given up on acting because he was tired of the small, unrewarding roles he was being offered. Y asked X to help by reading lines with other actors who were auditioning for his next film. X wasn't auditioning as the character ___ ______; he was just there to provide the "feed" lines. However, Y realized that X's dry, cynical delivery was exactly what his character needed and hence he shot with X first. A chance meeting went from installing doors to becoming the leading men in Hollywood. Id the actor X (5) and the director Y (5).
answer_text: X - Harrison Ford, Y - George Lucas

question_text: X's tenure as a goalkeeper for the Danish club Akademisk Boldklub (AB) in the early 1900s remains one of the most charming stories in sports history. While his brother Harald was a celebrated Olympic silver medalist, X was a competent but famously distracted shot-stopper. Legend has it that during a match against the German side Mittweida, X stood motionless as a long ball rolled toward his goal. He later admitted to teammates that he had been so engrossed in solving a problem that he had begun scribbling equations on the edge of the goalpost, proving that his mind was meant to solve other problems than his team's defence. Id X.

X, a known believer in Marxism utilized his influence as a lead actor to champion the dignity of labor within the Indian film industry. During an era when screen credits were reserved primarily for stars, X insisted that the contributions of technicians and junior artists be formally acknowledged. By making comprehensive credit lists a prerequisite for his participation in major films, he forced a shift in production standards, ensuring the "invisible" backbone of cinema received public recognition. Y single-handedly shattered the Hollywood Blacklist by publicly crediting Dalton Trumbo for the screenplay of the epic ______ in 1960. During the Cold War, blacklisted writers were forced to work under pseudonyms to avoid political persecution. Y's refusal to participate in this systemic censorship provided Trumbo with his first onscreen credit in a decade and Y continued with the part in the epic. This act of defiance effectively broke the red scare monopoly over the industry, restoring professional legitimacy to countless persecuted artists. Id X (5) and Y (5).
answer_text: X - Balraj Sahni, Y - Kirk Douglas

question_text: After his grueling, high-stakes work on the Manhattan Project, physicist X was severely burned out. He decided he would only do physics if it was fun. One day in the Cornell University cafeteria, he watched a student jokingly toss a plate into the air. X noticed that the Cornell logo on the plate was spinning faster than the plate was wobbling. Just for his own amusement, he sat down and calculated the mathematics of the plate's rotation. That purely playful calculation sparked a chain of thought that led directly to X diagrams and his Nobel Prize in QED. Id X.

During his incarceration by the British in the 1920s and 30s, authorities sought to break him by forcing him to wear heavy, rusted iron fetters on his legs. The irons in stock were undersized for him, rapidly rubbing the skin off his ankles and causing constant bleeding and intense pain. Rather than protesting or requesting the prison hospital, he used pure willpower to maintain his daily routine of hard labor and long walks in the yard. X's stoic refusal to show pain or compromise his posture became a massive psychological victory that deeply inspired his fellow revolutionaries across the subcontinent. Id X.

In 1968, X gave a presentation now known as "The Mother of All Demos." In 90 minutes, he debuted almost every element of modern computing. He demonstrated the first computer mouse, video conferencing, word processing, hypertext, and collaborative editing. While the demonstration was legendary among tech insiders, X's lab lost funding, and many of his researchers were poached by Xerox PARC (and later Apple). Because he was a researcher and not a businessman, others commercialized his ideas and became billionaires, while X remained a relatively obscure figure in the shadow of giants like Jobs and Gates. Id X.

Diamant glass, engineered by Saint-Gobain in the mid 80s, represents a peak in transparency. This extra-clear float glass is manufactured using a specialized process that utilizes sand with an exceptionally low iron content. By virtually eliminating the green tint characteristic of standard glass, it achieves a light transmission rate of over 90%, ensuring the removal of any tint or refraction allowing a near natural light pass through. Beyond its aesthetic purity, Diamant glass is highly versatile; it can be laminated, toughened, or curved, making it a preferred choice for buildings. Why or for what was the glass developed?

In the 1970s, the primary challenge for pacemakers was limited battery life, which forced patients into frequent surgeries. To solve this, scientists developed pacemakers powered by X. These tiny batteries offered a staggering theoretical lifespan of over 80 years compared the standard 3-4 years. While highly effective, they were eventually phased out in the 1980s due to the rise of more affordable lithium batteries and the complex regulatory burden of procurement and tracking. Remarkably, a few of these robust devices remain functional today, still pacing the hearts of their long-lived recipients. Id X.

In 1996, a group of powerful oligarchs known as the X orchestrated the survival of Y's presidency. Facing dismal approval ratings and a resurgent Communist Party, Y formed an unholy alliance with these tycoons, which included Boris Berezovsky, Mikhail Khodorkovsky, Vladimir Potanin, Vladimir Gusinsky, Alexander Smolensky, Petr Aven and Mikhail Fridman. In exchange for funding his campaign and providing favorable media coverage across their TV networks, the oligarchs demanded unprecedented influence. Through the "loans-for-shares" scheme, they acquired Russia's crown jewels, vast oil and metal industries, for fractions of their value. This effectively turned the Kremlin into a puppet office, where the X dictated national policy and economic transition. Id X (4) and Y (6).
answer_text: X - The Seven Bankers (Semibankirschina), Y - Boris Yeltsin

question_text: In the 1980s, an amateur chemist and hairdresser named Maurice Ward invented X, a plastic-like material that seemed to ignore the laws of thermodynamics. In a televised test, a laser that could burn through steel was aimed at a plastic egg coated in X. The egg remained cold and uncooked. It could withstand temperatures of 10,000 C. NASA and major tech firms were desperate for the recipe, but Ward was so paranoid about being cheated that he took the secret to his grave in 2011. While it "shouldn't work" for a simple home-brewed plastic to beat NASA's heat shields, recent attempts to reverse-engineer it suggest it was a complex mix of cornstarch, baking soda, and PVA glue. Id the material X which might remind you of a famous supe from an ongoing series.
answer_text: Starlite (the material), punning on "Starlight" from The Boys

The only known relief was chaulmoogra oil, but it was too thick to inject through thickened nerves and too nauseating to swallow. The president of her university, Arthur Dean, took her exact findings, published them without ever mentioning her name, and shamelessly dubbed it the "Dean Method." It took decades before records were corrected to honor the "Ball Method." Id the disease X.
